relevance_reason: Large Amish case series defining the clinical phenotype of NEDHCS caused by the homozygous SNIP1 p.Glu366Gly founder variant, with mapping, segregation, population frequency and transcriptome studies.

findings.statement: Ammous et al. (2021) described a complex autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder associated with a SNIP1 founder variant in the Amish, whose cardinal features include hypotonia, global developmental delay, intellectual disability, seizures, and a characteristic craniofacial appearance with skull abnormalities.
quotes: The cardinal clinical features of the condition include hypotonia, global developmental delay, intellectual disability, seizures, and a characteristic craniofacial appearance.
The cardinal clinical features of SNIP1-related disorder include: hypotonia, global developmental delay, intellectual disability, seizures, a characteristic facial appearance and skull abnormalities.

findings.statement: Ammous et al. (2021) evaluated 35 of 51 identified individuals from 21 interrelated Old Order Amish families (19 males, 16 females, aged 1 month to 26 years) with molecularly confirmed SNIP1-related disorder, including 2 previously reported individuals. All had severe nonverbal global developmental delay, hypotonia, hyporeflexia, seizures, feeding difficulties, abnormal skull shape, high-arched palate, and wide mouth with cupid's bow upper lip; other features included behavioral problems (75%), upper airway abnormalities (75%), congenital heart defects (60%), cardiomyopathy (12%), nystagmus/strabismus (45%), small for gestational age (54%), hypothyroidism (25%), and hypoglycemia (21%). Six children died between 9 months and 11 years, and substantial phenotypic variation was observed, including within sibships.
quotes: 35 of 51 identified individuals from 21 interrelated Old Order Amish families (19 males; 16 females, aged 1 month to 26 years) with molecularly confirmed SNIP1-related disorder were evaluated

Six children died between ages 9 months and 11 years as a consequence of infection, sudden cardiopulmonary arrest, or accidental drowning. Substantial phenotypic variation was observed between affected individuals, including within sibships.
| Congenital heart defects (ASD, VSD, aortic coarctation) | 60%

findings.statement: Ammous et al. (2021) reported craniofacial features including midface hypoplasia, wide mouth with downturned corners and thin cupid's bow upper lip, large tongue, high-arched palate, microretrognathia (Pierre Robin sequence with or without cleft palate in 3), malocclusion, small upturned bulbous nose, long palpebral fissures, and proptosis. Skull abnormalities ranged from normocephaly to severe multisuture craniosynostosis with cloverleaf skull in 5 individuals and included an irregular skull surface with variable calvarial thickness and bony dysplasia; other features were brachydactyly, broad thumbs, single palmar crease, clubfoot, pes planus, toenail hypoplasia, and pectus excavatum.
quotes: Craniofacial features (Fig 1A–1D) include midface hypoplasia, a wide mouth with downturned corners and thin cupids bow upper lip, large tongue, high arched palate, microretrognathia (Pierre Robin sequence with or without cleft palate in three patients), malocclusion, small upturned bulbous nose, long palpebral fissures and proptosis

Skull morphological abnormalities were observed and ranged from normocephaly to severe multi-suture craniosynostosis with Cloverleaf appearance of the skull in five individuals, and included an irregular skull surface with variable calvarium thickness and bony dysplasia
Other dysmorphic features include brachydactyly, broad thumbs, single palmar crease, congenital talipes equinovarus, pes planus, toenail hypoplasia and pectus excavatum

phenotypes.text: thin upper lip with cupid's bow

findings.statement: Ammous et al. (2021) found that all affected individuals developed epilepsy, with focal and generalized intractable seizures (myoclonic, absence, tonic-clonic) of infantile or childhood onset, abnormal EEG without characteristic pattern, seizures presenting as apnea in some infants, and drug-resistant epilepsy; some had developmental regression after status epilepticus, 2 with permanent hemiparesis. Most achieved independent ambulation (3-10 years), behavioral diagnoses included autism and attention deficit disorder, and all 18 with neuroimaging had abnormalities including hydrocephalus, ventriculomegaly, white matter abnormalities, thin corpus callosum, hypomyelination, Chiari malformation, absent septum pellucidum, and septo-optic dysplasia.
quotes: Seizure types include focal and generalised intractable seizures (myoclonic, absence, tonic-clonic) of infantile or childhood onset.
Some individuals suffered severe developmental regression following status epilepticus, with two reported to have subsequent permanent hemiparesis.

Neuroimaging was available for 18 individuals, all confirmed to have abnormalities, including hydrocephalus, ventriculomegaly, white matter abnormalities, thin corpus callosum, hypomyelination, irregular cortical ribbon, Chiari malformation, absence of the septum pellucidum, hypoplastic optic nerves and septo-optic dysplasia.

findings.statement: Ammous et al. (2021) reported congenital cardiac defects in 60% including hypoplastic left heart, aortic stenosis, bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, aortic root dilatation, ASD, VSD, PDA, and pulmonary artery stenosis, with left ventricular noncompaction cardiomyopathy in 12%. Neonatal upper airway difficulties (laryngomalacia, pharyngomalacia, subglottic stenosis) sometimes required tracheostomy; poor neonatal feeding was universal, with many requiring gastrostomy, and other features included intestinal malrotation, IUGR, hypoglycemia, hypothyroidism, strabismus, nystagmus, myopia, and hearing loss.
quotes: including hypoplastic left heart syndrome, aortic stenosis and bicuspid aortic valve, aortic coarctation, aortic root dilatation, atrial septal defect (ASD), ventricular septal defect (VSD), patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), pulmonary artery stenosis and mitral valve regurgitation, 12% of affected individuals developed cardiomyopathy (left ventricular noncompaction)
including laryngomalacia, pharyngomalacia and subglottic stenosis of variable severity, causing a weak cry, stridor and apnea, occasionally requiring tracheostomy and supplementary home oxygen
Poor feeding in the neonatal period is universal and many require a gastrostomy tube to both aid nutrition and reduce risk of aspiration pneumonia.

findings.statement: Ammous et al. (2021) performed genome-wide SNP homozygosity mapping in 4 affected individuals from 2 Amish nuclear families and identified a single shared 1.65-Mb region of homozygosity on chromosome 1p34.3 between rs6667450 and rs10889902, containing 17 genes.
quotes: a small (1.65Mb) genomic region on chromosome 1p34.3 delimited by SNP markers rs6667450 and rs10889902 (NC_000001.11:g.36,492,230–38,143,653; S1 Fig), highly likely to contain the disease locus, comprising 17 genes

findings.statement: In Amish individuals with NEDHCS, Ammous et al. (2021) identified by whole-exome sequencing a homozygous c.1097A>G (p.Glu366Gly) variant in exon 4 of the SNIP1 gene, previously reported by Puffenberger et al. (2012), within the 1p34.3 interval. Homozygosity was confirmed in 35 individuals; all parents were heterozygous and unaffected sibs were heterozygous or wildtype. The residue is highly conserved and lies near the C-terminal FHA domain; the variant was found in gnomAD at 0.001% (11 heterozygotes, 10 Amish, no homozygotes) and was classified as pathogenic.
quotes: WES data on two individuals (X:16 and X:42) identified only a single potentially pathogenic sequence variant (Chr1:g.37537842T>C; RefSeq NM_024700.4:c.1097A>G, p.(Glu366Gly) [hg38]) in exon four of the SNIP1 gene
confirmed homozygosity of the SNIP1 variant in 35 individuals, with all parents being heterozygous for the variant and all unaffected siblings being heterozygous for the variant or wild type
The variant is present in gnomAD (v3.1) with an allele frequency of 0.001% with 11 heterozygotes (10 Amish) and no homozygous individuals listed

findings.statement: Ammous et al. (2021) found the SNIP1 c.1097A>G (p.Glu366Gly) founder variant at an allele frequency of 0.5% in Pennsylvania Amish and 1.4% in Ohio/Indiana/Wisconsin Amish in a control database of more than 5,000 individuals, with no unaffected homozygotes. In total 51 Old Order Amish individuals from 27 sibships were identified with the disorder, 49 confirmed homozygous; 12 were deceased (age at death 1 week to 11 years).
quotes: determined that the SNIP1 NM_024700.4:c.1097A>G, p.(Glu366Gly) variant is present at an allele frequency of between 0.5% (Pennsylvania Amish) and 1.4% (Ohio/Indiana/Wisconsin Amish) in this founder population, with no unaffected individuals being homozygous for this variant
A total of fifty-one Old Order Amish individuals were identified with SNIP1-related disorder, among 27 sibships.
Seventy-six percent (n = 39) are currently living (age range 6 months to 30 years), while 24% (n = 12) are deceased (age of death between 1 week and 11 years).

findings.statement: Ammous et al. (2021) performed whole-blood transcriptome sequencing in 6 affected individuals from 4 sibships versus sex-matched controls and identified 75 significantly upregulated and 109 downregulated genes, many associated with neurologic disease (e.g., ROBO1, the most upregulated gene, and CNTNAP2 and SYT1). Reactome analysis showed TGF-beta receptor signaling in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition as the most overrepresented pathway. The authors suggested that the variant disrupts regulation of multiple signaling pathways, and noted that because Snip1-null mice are embryonic lethal, the variant may be unlikely to cause complete loss of function.
quotes: Differentially expressed genes with a false discovery rate (FDR) adjusted p-value of <0.05 identified a list of 75 significantly upregulated genes, and 109 significantly downregulated genes

the most overrepresented pathway was the TGF-β receptor signalling in epithelial to mesenchyme pathway with differential expression of three genes (upregulation of PARD3 and downregulation of F11R and RPS27A)
SNIP1 null mouse models display embryonic lethality indicating that this Amish variant may be unlikely to result in complete loss of function

findings.statement: Ammous et al. (2021) recommended elective gastrostomy tube placement, careful optimization of anticonvulsants to treat infantile apnea and prevent status epilepticus, early EEG in infants with apneic episodes, neuroimaging and echocardiography at diagnosis, monitoring for hypoglycemia and hypothyroidism, early supportive therapies, and yearly ophthalmology and audiology assessments. No antiepileptic medication consistently provided effective seizure control.
quotes: We recommend elective gastrostomy tube placement to support growth and limit pulmonary aspiration, as well as careful optimisation of anticonvulsant medications to treat apnea in infancy, maintain seizure control, and prevent status epilepticus and consequent developmental regression.

There were no antiepileptic medications identified that consistently provide effective seizure control (defined as manageable frequency of seizures) and several individuals display multiple drug resistant epilepsy.

relevance_reason: The paper describes the Amish disorder 'symptomatic epilepsy and skull dysplasia' (psychomotor retardation, epilepsy, craniofacial dysmorphism). It reports the clinical features, maps the locus to chromosome 1, identifies the homozygous SNIP1 p.Glu366Gly variant and includes functional studies.

findings.statement: Puffenberger et al. (2012) described Old Order Amish children with symptomatic epilepsy and skull dysplasia. Affected neonates were hypotonic and fed poorly. Over time they developed dysmorphic features: bulbous nose, wide mouth and tongue, broad jaw with protuberant angles, short hands, short tapered fingers and broad thumbs. The children had severe psychomotor delay and did not learn to walk or speak; they did not engage socially or follow verbal commands.
quotes: Affected neonates are hypotonic and feed poorly. Dysmorphic features that evolve over time include a bulbous nose, wide mouth and tongue, broad jaw with protuberant angles, short hands, short tapered fingers, and broad thumbs (Figure 3, A).
Affected children have severe psychomotor delay and do not learn to walk or speak.
Some children show behavioral responses to language, but they do not socially engage or follow verbal commands.

findings.statement: Puffenberger et al. (2012) reported that on examination affected children typically had strabismus, slow horizontal nystagmus, hypotonia, and weak or absent tendon reflexes. Brain MRI showed ventriculomegaly, a thin corpus callosum, white matter abnormalities (hypomyelination), and an undulating or 'lumpy' skull surface, with the cortical ribbon following the irregular skull contour.
quotes: Examination typically reveals a subdued child with strabismus, slow horizontal nystagmus, hypotonia, and weak or absent tendon reflexes.
Magnetic resonance imaging reveals ventriculomegaly, thin corpus callosum, white matter abnormalities, and an undulating or “lumpy” skull surface (Figure 3, E).
MRI showed enlarged ventricles, a thin corpus callosum, hypomyelination, and an irregular, undulating skull surface.

findings.statement: Puffenberger et al. (2012) reported that multifocal spike-wave discharges from central, occipital and temporal regions typically began by 6 months of age. They were accompanied by intractable focal or generalized seizures, including dystonic posturing, drop attacks, myoclonic jerks and generalized tonic-clonic events. Some patients had subglottic stenosis, aortic stenosis, bicuspid aortic valve, umbilical hernia, or hydrocele.
quotes: Multifocal spike-wave discharges from central, occipital, and temporal regions typically begin by 6 months of age and are accompanied by focal or generalized seizures that can manifest as dystonic posturing, drop attacks, myoclonic jerks, or generalized tonic-clonic events.
Multiple intractable seizure types can afflict an individual patient.
Physical anomalies found in some patients include subglottic stenosis, aortic stenosis, bicuspid aortic valve, umbilical hernia, and hydrocele.

findings.statement: Puffenberger et al. (2012) used autozygosity mapping with 10K SNP arrays in 6 affected Amish individuals to map symptomatic epilepsy and skull dysplasia to a 6.6-Mb shared homozygous region on chromosome 1 between rs2153337 and rs2225251. The region contained 126 genes.
quotes: Symptomatic epilepsy and skull dysplasia | 6 | 1 | rs2153337 | rs2225251 | 6.6 | 126
Using between 2 and 9 samples, we genetically mapped five disorders using 10 K SNP arrays

findings.statement: Puffenberger et al. (2012) performed exome sequencing in 3 affected individuals from 2 sibships with symptomatic epilepsy and skull dysplasia. Of 34 homozygous variants in the mapped region, the only novel one was SNIP1 c.1097A>G (p.Glu366Gly), which PolyPhen-2 predicted to be probably damaging. The variant was confirmed by Sanger sequencing and checked for segregation. Screening of 203 Old Order Amish controls found 5 carriers (2.5%) and no homozygotes. Glu366 is highly conserved and lies in the C-terminal region where SNIP1 interacts with c-Myc, Smad1 and Smad2.
quotes: Exome data on three affected individuals from two sibships revealed 34 homozygous variants in the mapped region. Of these, only one was novel, SNIP1 c.1097A>G (p.Glu366Gly) (Table 3).
An unlabeled probe melting analysis for this variant identified 5 carriers among 203 Old Order Amish controls (2.5%) (Table 4).
SNIP1 Glu366 is highly conserved and the p.Glu366Gly mutation is in the C-terminus where SNIP1 interacts with c-Myc [48], Smad1 and Smad2 [46], [49].

findings.statement: Puffenberger et al. (2012) studied the mouse equivalent of the human SNIP1 variant, Snip1 p.Glu353Gly (c.1058A>G), in transfected mIMCD3 cells. Its transcript was expressed at levels comparable to wild type. Wild-type Snip1 localized to the nucleus in a punctate pattern, whereas the mutant protein looked more aggregated. On Western blotting the mutant protein was unstable, with band density 84.9% lower than wild type.
quotes: Reverse transcriptase-PCR suggests that the Snip1 c.1058A>G (corresponding to human SNIP1 c.1097A>G) transcript is expressed at levels comparable to wild-type (Figure 3, F).

However, Snip1 p.Glu353Gly (corresponding to human p.Glu366Gly) had a more aggregated appearance (Figure 3, E) and Western blotting proved it unstable (Figure 3, F); its band density was 84.9±9.6% SD lower than wild-type (n = 4 independent transfections each).

findings.statement: Puffenberger et al. (2012) proposed that reduced SNIP1 abundance probably lowers c-Myc activity and raises TGF-beta and NF-kappa-B signaling. They noted that disrupting c-Myc or CBP/p300 signaling in mice can cause abnormal development of the brain, skull, craniofacial bones and distal limbs, and that increased TGF-beta/Smad2 or NF-kappa-B signaling in mouse brain can each initiate epileptogenesis.
quotes: Decreased abundance of SNIP1 likely results in decreased c-Myc activity and increased TGF-β and NF-κB signaling.
Disruption of c-Myc or CBP/p300 signaling in mice can result in abnormal development of the brain, skull, craniofacial bones, and distal limbs [50], [51], [52], [53], [54].
